hunga-tonga-new-island.story: Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai was a small volcanic island in Tonga, in the South Pacific, about 65 kilometres north of Tonga's main island, Tongatapu. It began as two separate islands, Hunga Tonga and Hunga Haʻapai, about 1.6 kilometres apart on the rim of an undersea volcano. An eruption in 2014 and 2015 piled up new ground that joined them into one island, with a strip of deposits 380 metres wide, called a tombolo, linking them along one side. The highest point reached 149 metres. Surveys in 2019 found ferns, guava trees, mosses and sedges, along with cockroaches, moths, rats and spiders, and seabirds were breeding there. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets out states' rights at sea, defines an island as land formed naturally, surrounded by water and above high tide, and for about seven years this ground met that test. In January 2022 the volcano erupted again, sending a plume 58 kilometres high and a tsunami as far as Japan and the Americas. The eruption destroyed most of the joined island, and only small remnants of the two original islands are left.
hunga-tonga-new-island.mechanism: Under Article 121 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, land formed naturally and standing above high tide counts as an island. It keeps that status only as long as it stays above the water.
hunga-tonga-new-island.stopped_by: The volcano's eruption of January 2022, which destroyed most of the island

nishinoshima-growth.story: Nishinoshima is a volcanic island belonging to Japan, about 940 kilometres south-southeast of Tokyo and 130 kilometres from the nearest inhabited island in the Ogasawara chain. Before 1973 it was a small green island. On 30 May 1973 a fishing boat told the Japan Coast Guard it had seen white smoke rising nearby. The Coast Guard flew over the same day and kept surveying from the air as new land formed. By August 1974 it put the new land at about 316,000 square metres, and erosion and shifting sand then joined it to the old island. A further eruption began in November 2013 and built another islet to the southeast. Officials said they would name it once it was stable, but it merged with the main island first. By July 2016 a volcanic cone stood about 142 metres high, and more eruptions followed in 2020, 2021 and 2022. Because a Japanese agency watched each stage and the new ground grew onto an island Japan already held, it was simply added to Japanese territory. No other claim to it is recorded.
nishinoshima-growth.mechanism: When new land grows onto an island a state already holds, it adds to that state's territory, so no separate question of ownership arises.

south-talpatti-new-moore.story: South Talpatti, which India called New Moore, was a low sandbar in the Bay of Bengal, claimed by both India and Bangladesh. It formed from silt after the Bhola cyclone of November 1970, and a US satellite picked it up in 1974 at about 2,500 square metres. It later grew to about 10,000 square metres at low tide and never stood more than 2 metres above the sea. The sandbar mattered because it lay 2 kilometres from the mouth of the Hariabhanga River, which marks the border between the two countries. Their boundary follows the river's main channel, so ownership depended on which side of the sandbar the channel ran, and each country relied on its own surveys. India reportedly raised its flag in 1981 and set up a temporary Border Security Force base. Neither country built anything lasting, because floods in the river delta reshaped the ground every year. In October 2009 Bangladesh took the wider sea boundary dispute to arbitration, meaning a panel of judges the parties agree to obey. In March 2010 an Indian oceanographer reported the island had disappeared. The final award of 7 July 2014 gave Bangladesh 19,467 of the 25,000 square kilometres of disputed sea and placed the site of the vanished sandbar on India's side.
south-talpatti-new-moore.mechanism: A sandbar too low and unstable to settle can still matter because it might move a sea boundary. An arbitration tribunal, a panel of judges chosen to settle a dispute, ruled on this one's position after it had gone under the sea.
south-talpatti-new-moore.challenge: Bangladesh took the dispute to arbitration in October 2009, and the final award came in July 2014
south-talpatti-new-moore.recognition: The arbitration award placed the site on the Indian side
south-talpatti-new-moore.stopped_by: Rising seas and erosion removed the sandbar, and the 2014 arbitration award settled the boundary

surtsey-paris-match.story: Surtsey is a volcanic island off the south coast of Iceland that rose from the sea in an eruption beginning in November 1963. The cook of the Icelandic trawler Ísleifur II saw dark smoke on 14 November, and the crew found the eruption breaking the surface. An Icelandic naming committee called the new island Surtsey, after a fire giant in Norse myth. On 6 December three French journalists from the magazine Paris Match landed and stayed about 15 minutes, until explosions drove them off. They jokingly claimed the island for France, and Iceland quickly stated that it belonged to Iceland. The eruption lasted until 5 June 1967. Hard lava capped the loose ash, so the island survived where many others wash away, and its highest point then was 174 metres. In 1965, while the eruption was still going on, Iceland declared the island a nature reserve so that scientists could watch life arrive on bare rock. That rule still applies. Only a few scientists may land, and everyone else can see it closely only from a small plane, so no one has been able to settle there.
surtsey-paris-match.mechanism: New land off a coastal state's shore is treated as that state's from the start. The state can then close it with a conservation order before anyone settles.
surtsey-paris-match.challenge: A joking French claim by magazine journalists, answered at once by Iceland

zalzala-koh.story: Zalzala Koh was a small island that appeared in the Arabian Sea off Pakistan on 24 September 2013, within hours of a 7.7-magnitude earthquake in the province of Balochistan. Its name means 'Earthquake Mountain' in Urdu. It stood about 2 kilometres from shore near Gwadar and the Hingol area, close enough to be seen from the coast. It may have been a mud volcano, and the head of Pakistan's National Institute of Oceanography said gas escaping from the seabed had caused it. Satellite measurements put it at about 175 metres by 160 metres and 15 to 20 metres high, though those figures were debated. Its surface was lifeless, but fish and coral gathered around it, which helped local fishing. Geologists predicted it would not last. It sank 3 metres within a month and had gone by the end of 2016. Because it rose so close to the coast it lay inside Pakistan's territorial sea, the belt of water a coastal state controls, so no one else could have claimed it.
zalzala-koh.mechanism: A coastal state owns the seabed under its territorial sea, the belt of water next to its coast, under Article 2 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Land rising 2 kilometres offshore therefore comes up on that state's own territory.
zalzala-koh.stopped_by: It sank and eroded away by the end of 2016

global-country-of-world-peace.story: The Global Country of World Peace is a non-profit organisation that calls itself a world government without borders. Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, the founder of Transcendental Meditation, launched it on 7 October 2000, and it was incorporated in Iowa in the United States in 2002. It promotes meditation and education and builds what it calls 'buildings for peace' in major cities. It is run by 'rajas', initiates said to hold spiritual authority over a nation, and reports say that title cost $1 million or more. The group tried to buy land where it could be sovereign, and every attempt failed. In 2000 it offered Suriname $1.3 billion over three years for a 200-year lease of 3,500 acres, and no deal followed. Tuvalu rejected a proposed city-state near its airport in 2001, and Rota in the Northern Mariana Islands declined a request for 100 acres in 2002. Costa Rica expelled its representative in 2002 after officials said to be acting for the group allegedly offered Talamanca families payments to appoint a king. The group did buy ordinary private property, including a 30-acre island in Ireland and more than 1,000 acres in Kansas for a planned capital, all of it under the law of the country concerned. It also issued a currency, the raam, accepted by some businesses in Iowa and the Netherlands. The neurologist Tony Nader leads it, and its headquarters are in Maharishi Vedic City, Iowa.
global-country-of-world-peace.mechanism: Buying land gives a private owner title to it, while the country it lies in keeps governing it. Sovereignty, the right to govern a territory, has to be granted by a state, and every state the group approached refused.

add_sources.t: Global Country of World Peace, Wikipedia

set.anchor: No territory of its own; headquarters in Maharishi Vedic City, Iowa

nova-roma.story: Nova Roma is an international non-profit organisation that aims to restore the religion, culture and values of ancient Rome. It was formed in 1998 and later incorporated in the US state of Maine, and it offers a community for re-enactors, scholars and fans of ancient Rome. It calls itself a sovereign nation and is organised like the Roman Republic, with a senate, elected officials and laws passed by members' votes. Latin is its official language, ancient Roman religion is its state religion alongside a guarantee of freedom of religion, and groups in different countries can form local branches called provinces. It minted coins in 2000 and 2005. Some outside observers class it as a micronation, a small self-declared state that other states do not recognise. It claims no territory, and its members go on living under the laws of their own countries. Its most recent dated activity on record is a twentieth-anniversary celebration in Rome, and no report confirms what it does now.
nova-roma.mechanism: Calling a group a sovereign nation has no legal effect when it holds no territory. In law Nova Roma is a non-profit organisation registered in Maine.

set.anchor: No territory claimed; incorporated in Maine, USA

nutopia.story: Nutopia was a country with no land, announced by the musician John Lennon and the artist Yoko Ono at a press conference in New York City on 2 April 1973, the day after they signed its declaration. The text says Nutopia has no land, no boundaries, no passports, only people, and no laws other than cosmic ones. Anyone could become a citizen by declaring awareness of it. All citizens were to be ambassadors, and the founders asked for diplomatic immunity, the legal protection foreign diplomats have from a host country's courts, along with recognition from the United Nations. Lennon had just received an order to leave the United States, and the new country was partly a way to answer it. Nutopia's flag was a white handkerchief, and its anthem, on Lennon's 1973 album Mind Games, is four seconds of silence. Its embassy was an apartment at 1 White Street in Manhattan and later a plaque on a kitchen door at the Dakota building. No record shows any government granting the immunity. The deportation order was overturned in 1975 and Lennon received a green card, the US permit for permanent residence, in 1976. Since April 2024 people have been able to declare citizenship through a website.
nutopia.mechanism: A declaration alone gives no one diplomatic immunity, because that protection comes from the state hosting a diplomat. Lennon's position changed only when US authorities overturned the deportation order in 1975.
nutopia.laws: No laws except 'cosmic' ones, by its own declaration
nutopia.recognition: None; the founders asked the UN to recognise it

obsidia.story: The Ambulatory Free States of Obsidia is a feminist micronation, a small self-declared state that no government recognises, founded in 2015 by Karo Yagjian, who holds the title Grand Marshal. Yagjian was inspired partly by a summit of micronations called MicroCon and took a piece of obsidian, a black volcanic rock, and declared it independent. The nation's whole territory is two slabs of obsidian about the size of a book, carried in a blue and pink briefcase usually based in Oakland, California. It is described as a mobile nation and art project that promotes gender equality and LGBTQ rights and opposes capitalism and borders. Anyone can become a citizen by reciting an oath and performing a salute, though cisgender men cannot serve in its government. In November 2021 Huck magazine estimated about 250 citizens, roughly 50 with passports, and reported satellite embassies in Hong Kong and Germany. No later report confirms its present activity.
obsidia.mechanism: A territory that fits in a briefcase is a claim that travels with objects. The law of whichever country the briefcase is in continues to apply to the people carrying it.

add_sources.t: Inside the anti-capitalist, anti-border micronation, Huck

obsidia.why: Huck magazine names the founder as Karo Yagjian; the source list had Carolyn Yagjian.

set.anchor: No fixed location; the briefcase holding its territory is usually in Oakland, California

bishop-ring.story: The Bishop Ring is a design for an enormous space habitat, a spinning wheel with people living on its inner surface. Forrest Bishop of the Institute of Atomic-Scale Engineering proposed it in 1997 in a paper called Open Air Space Habitats. The ring would have a radius of about 1,000 kilometres and a width of 500 kilometres, giving about 3 million square kilometres of living space, close to the size of Argentina or India. Its spin would produce artificial gravity, and that force together with walls about 200 kilometres high would hold in the air, so it would need no roof. The size depends on carbon nanotubes, a very strong material made of carbon atoms, in place of the steel used in designs from the 1970s. Bishop considered placing it at the Sun-Earth L4 and L5 points, which are stable spots in Earth's orbit 60 degrees ahead of and behind Earth, or closer to the Sun, or in the asteroid belt or beyond. It has stayed on paper, and no one has tried to build it.
bishop-ring.mechanism: Under Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the state that registers an object sent into space keeps legal control over it. However large it was, a habitat like this would still count as one space object under the law of the state that registered it.

set.anchor: A design with no site on Earth; no marker coordinate

edwards-sea-anchored-elevator.story: This was a plan for a space elevator, a cable running from the ground into space and held taut by a counterweight, with climbing machines carrying cargo up and down it. From 2000 the scientist Bradley Edwards worked on a version using a thin, wide ribbon of carbon nanotube composite, a very strong material made of carbon atoms. NASA's advanced concepts institute supported the work, which involved more than 20 institutions and 50 participants. He suggested anchoring the ribbon in the western equatorial Pacific to avoid lightning and hurricanes, on a movable sea platform that could shift the ribbon out of the way of space debris large enough to track. Construction would begin with a seed cable of 19,800 kilograms, and 207 climbers would then add material until the ribbon reached about 750 tons and could lift 20 tons per climber. Ocean sites are usually in international waters, which could make negotiations over territory simpler. Philip Ragan, co-author of a book on space elevators, said the first country to deploy one could control most space activities. The material has never been made at the strength and length required, and the elevator was never built.
edwards-sea-anchored-elevator.mechanism: Putting the base on the high seas, the ocean outside any country's control, avoids needing a host country. Under Articles VII and VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, the state that launches or registers the elevator would still be liable for damage and would keep legal control of it.

kalpana-one.story: Kalpana One is a design for a space settlement, a permanent home in space with more extensive living quarters than a space station. It was revised in 2007 in a paper by Al Globus. The design is a short spinning cylinder with a radius of 250 metres and a length of 325 metres, sized for 3,000 residents. Its spin would simulate gravity, and smaller cylinders inside would hold farms and recreation areas. Radiation shielding of 10 metric tons per square metre would turn with the habitat. It belongs to a family of similar designs, among them Lewis One, also by Globus, and the McKendree cylinder of 1995, which has a radius of 460 kilometres. Designers once favoured the Moon's L4 and L5 points, stable spots 60 degrees ahead of and behind the Moon in its orbit. Those points are now thought too far from the Moon and Earth, and a settlement there would spend about two-thirds of its time outside the protection of Earth's magnetic field. A different orbit timed to the Moon, called a two-to-one resonance orbit, has been proposed. No space settlement has been built.
kalpana-one.mechanism: Under Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the state that registers an object sent into space keeps legal control over it. Any such settlement would therefore live under that state's law.

set.anchor: A design with no site on Earth; no marker coordinate

liftport.story: LiftPort Group is a private company in Washington state, founded in April 2003 by Michael Laine, that set out to build a space elevator, a cable running from the ground into space with climbing machines carrying cargo along it. In 2005 it announced a plant in Millville, New Jersey, to make carbon nanotubes, a very strong material made of carbon atoms, and set a goal of launching an elevator in 2010. The plant was never built. It did run tests, including a 1,000-foot ribbon held up by a balloon in September 2005 with a machine climbing it, and in February 2006 it reported testing a mile of tether made of carbon fibre and fibreglass. In 2007 the company faced a penalty over an alleged illegal offering of its shares, and in February 2010 it settled with the State of Washington without a fine. In 2011 Laine turned to an elevator on the Moon as a first step, and a 2012 Kickstarter campaign raised $110,353 from 3,468 backers. Wikipedia reports that many of them have asked what happened and received no reply. In April 2019 Laine admitted that little progress had been made despite more than $200,000 in seed funding. No elevator has been built.
liftport.mechanism: A space elevator would need approval from whichever state controlled its base, but the company never got far enough for any state to have to decide. The only legal action it met concerned the sale of its shares.
liftport.cost: Over $200,000 in seed funding, plus $110,353 from Kickstarter
liftport.why: Company founded April 2003, earlier than the listed 2005, which was the date of the plant announcement.

obayashi-space-elevator.story: This is a plan by Obayashi, a large Japanese construction company, to build a space elevator, a cable running from the ground into space with climbing vehicles carrying cargo and people along it. In 2012 the company announced that it could build one by 2050 using carbon nanotubes, a very strong material made of carbon atoms. A passenger vehicle would take 8 days to reach geosynchronous orbit, the height at which a satellite keeps pace with Earth's rotation. Obayashi published further details in 2016, and a report in 2018 described a small first test, with no outcome recorded. The material remains the main obstacle. A study by Feng Ding's team in 2016 suggested that small flaws could sharply cut the strength of nanotubes, and Google X, Google's research division, put its own elevator project in what it called deep freeze after finding that no one had made a perfect strand longer than a metre. Nothing has been built so far.
obayashi-space-elevator.mechanism: An elevator is fixed to Earth at its base, so the country hosting the base, or the law of the high seas if it stands in open ocean, would set the terms before any space law applied.

stanford-torus.story: The Stanford torus is a design for a wheel-shaped space colony, drawn up during a NASA summer study at Stanford University in California in 1975. The results appeared in 1977 as Space Settlements: A Design Study by Richard Johnson and Charles Holbrow. The purpose was to work out how people might live permanently in space. The ring would be about 1.8 kilometres across, with a living tube 130 metres wide, for 10,000 permanent residents. It would turn once a minute, and the spin would give people on the inner surface of the outer ring about the same gravity as Earth. Mirrors would bring in sunlight through windows. Total mass would be about 10 million metric tons, and about 95% of that would be a radiation shield of raw soil from the Moon. It would sit at the Earth-Moon L5 point, a stable spot in the Moon's orbit 60 degrees behind the Moon. It was never built, though a 2012 paper adapted the design for a generation ship, a ship meant to carry people for lifetimes.
stanford-torus.mechanism: Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming the Moon and other bodies in space, but a colony in open space would stand on none of them. The rule that matters more here is Article VIII, which gives legal control to the state that registers the object.

artemis-project-europa.story: In 1997 the private Artemis Project drafted a plan to settle Europa, a moon of Jupiter whose surface is ice over a hidden ocean. It proposed igloos on the surface as bases for drilling through the ice to explore the ocean below, and it suggested people could live in air pockets inside the ice. That ocean may hold more than twice the water of all Earth's oceans, but metals and minerals would have to be brought in. Radiation is the main barrier. An unshielded person would take about 5.40 sieverts a day, a measure of radiation dose, when about 5 sieverts over a few days is fatal. Heavy shielding might make a research base possible. The plan was never carried out.
artemis-project-europa.mechanism: Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty makes each state answer for its citizens' activities in space, so a private plan would need a state's authorisation and supervision. No such approval is recorded.

set.anchor: A design with no site on Earth; no marker coordinate

janhunen-ceres-megasatellite.story: This is a design for a large space settlement in high orbit around Ceres, the dwarf planet in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. It was set out by Pekka Janhunen, a Finnish space physicist at the Finnish Meteorological Institute, in a preprint, a paper shared before formal publication, posted in November 2020 and revised in May 2021. He chose Ceres mainly for its nitrogen, which an Earth-like atmosphere requires. Spinning habitats joined to a disk-shaped frame by magnetic bearings would give the same gravity as Earth, and mirrors would bring in sunlight. Population density would stay at 500 people per square kilometre, on soil 1.5 metres deep that could be deepened to 4 metres. Each person would account for about 10 million kilograms of material, mostly soil and radiation shielding. The stated aim is a long-lasting world in which all atoms are recycled. A space elevator on Ceres would lift material cheaply, which the author considers feasible because of the planet's low gravity and fast rotation. It remains a paper design.
janhunen-ceres-megasatellite.mechanism: The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming bodies in space. Whether mining a body counts as claiming it is unsettled, and a settlement built from Ceres's material would depend on the answer.

set.anchor: Helsinki, where the author's institute is based

nasa-hope-callisto.story: HOPE, short for Revolutionary Concepts for Human Outer Planet Exploration, was a NASA study in 2003 of how people might reach the outer planets. It chose Callisto, a moon of Jupiter, because Callisto orbits outside Jupiter's radiation belt, the zone of harmful radiation that surrounds the planet. A base on the surface could make fuel for further exploration of the solar system. Callisto has accessible water, silicate rock and metals, gravity of about 0.13 of Earth's, and probably an ocean inside it. A crew's round trip was estimated at about 2 to 5 years, assuming major advances in propulsion. The work stopped at the study stage, and no mission followed.
nasa-hope-callisto.mechanism: Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming a moon as their own. A state base would be legal only as long as it did not amount to such a claim.

set.anchor: NASA Headquarters, Washington DC, standing for the agency

titan-settlement-proposals.story: Titan, the largest moon of Saturn, has been proposed as a site for human settlement. The main advocate is Robert Zubrin, an American aerospace engineer and founder of the Mars Society, who wrote in his 1999 book Entering Space that Saturn is the most valuable of the giant planets and Titan the best moon for a base. His reasons were that Saturn is relatively close, has low radiation and has a good system of moons. Stephen Gillett had written about Titan as a home for life in the magazine Analog in 1992. Titan's nitrogen and methane atmosphere could supply a gas for making breathing air, and water beneath the surface could yield oxygen. Radar studies published in 2008 by Ralph Lorenz's team found hundreds of times Earth's known oil and gas reserves in hydrocarbons, and its lakes span about 1 to 100 kilometres. The objections are extreme cold, a lack of free oxygen for chemical power, and gravity about one-seventh of Earth's, with unknown effects on bone, muscle and children's growth. No one has gone past proposals on paper.
titan-settlement-proposals.mechanism: The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars nations from claiming bodies in space. States disagree over whether extracting resources counts as claiming, so any plan built on Titan's hydrocarbons would face that open question.

set.anchor: Lakewood, Colorado, headquarters of Pioneer Energy, a company Zubrin founded

abalonia-cortes-bank.story: Abalonia was a planned country on Cortes Bank, a shallow undersea mountain about 111 miles off San Diego, California, whose highest point, Bishop Rock, lies just under the surface. In 1966 a team of entrepreneurs including Jim Houtz planned to turn it into a constitutional monarchy. They reasoned that because the bank lay in international waters, maritime law would let them rule their own nation. A newspaper first reported the plan on 31 October 1966 under the headline 'Pair Planning Island Nation off San Diego'. They would sink a concrete-hulled Second World War freighter, the SS Jalisco, on Bishop Rock, surround it with a growing ring of boulders and use it as a seafood processing plant. The ship was towed out from San Francisco, but waves broke it apart on the rock and the crew were nearly killed. Houtz, who was aboard and was injured, later told the writer Chris Dixon that the affair cost him his marriage and left him in financial ruin. The wreck lies in three pieces in 6 to 40 feet of water. When another company later proposed a nation called Taluga on the same bank, the US government declared it US territory as part of the continental shelf, the shallow seabed extending from a country's coast.
abalonia-cortes-bank.mechanism: A coastal state has exclusive rights over the resources of its continental shelf, the shallow seabed off its coast. The US used that rule against later plans for this bank, and the same rule stopped similar projects off Florida.
abalonia-cortes-bank.challenge: The sea destroyed the ship before any state acted
abalonia-cortes-bank.stopped_by: Waves destroyed the ship; the US later declared the bank part of its continental shelf

autopia-saya-de-malha.story: Autopia was a planned micronation, a small self-declared state, on the Saya de Malha Bank, a huge underwater plateau in the Indian Ocean southeast of the Seychelles, less than 33 feet deep in places. The people behind it were the architect Wolf Hilbertz and the marine biologist Thomas Goreau. Hilbertz had patented Biorock, a process that uses a weak electric current to deposit limestone on sunken steel, and he hoped to grow homes this way for a self-sufficient settlement belonging to its residents. The name meant 'the place that builds itself'. He said most of the bank lay on the high seas, the ocean outside any country's control, governed only by the UN Law of the Sea, and reporter Ian Urbina describes it as hundreds of miles beyond any nation's reach. Wikipedia says differently, that Mauritius administers the whole bank because part of it lies in Mauritius's exclusive economic zone, the 200-mile belt where a coastal state controls resources. On 9 March 1997 the two men sailed three days from Victoria in the Seychelles with solar panels, metal scaffolding and cornerstones. In 2002 they returned in three sailboats with architects, cartographers and marine biologists. With a cyclone approaching, they built a steel frame five by five metres and two metres high in six days, kept charged by a small battery. The plans then stalled for lack of money.
autopia-saya-de-malha.mechanism: Open ocean belongs to no state, so the founders expected no legal obstacle on a mid-ocean bank. Any part of the bank within 200 miles of a state's coast falls in that state's exclusive economic zone, where it controls resources.
autopia-saya-de-malha.challenge: Not tested. Founders said the bank was on the high seas, while part of it lies in Mauritius's exclusive economic zone
autopia-saya-de-malha.why: Entry stated the site was beyond national jurisdiction; Wikipedia reports part of the bank lies in Mauritius's exclusive economic zone and that Mauritius administers it. Both views are now attributed.

grand-capri-atlantis-isle-of-gold.story: Grand Capri Republic and Atlantis, Isle of Gold were two rival plans to found new countries on Triumph and Long Reefs, two coral reefs about four and a half miles off southeast Florida near Miami. The reefs are underwater except for brief exposure at low tide, and they lay in international waters at the time, so the promoters believed no state could stop them. Louis M. Ray and his firm, Acme General Contractors, planned Grand Capri. They placed caissons, large watertight boxes, on the reefs and filled them with material dredged from the seabed. A rival, Atlantis Development Corporation, said an earlier discovery gave it better title and planned commercial buildings on pilings. On 16 November 1964 Acme applied to the US Army Corps of Engineers, the federal agency that regulates building in waterways, to build a 20-acre resort island. The Corps refused, and Ray dredged anyway. A trial court ordered a temporary halt in April 1965. In January 1969 it barred construction but rejected the government's trespass claim, because the government did not own the reefs. The government appealed. In 1970 the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit held that the reefs were part of the outer continental shelf, the seabed extending from the coast, where US law and the Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf give the United States exclusive rights to explore and exploit resources. It ordered a full permanent ban on construction, noting harm to corals and to shipping.
grand-capri-atlantis-isle-of-gold.mechanism: United States v. Ray (1970) held that a coastal state can stop building on its continental shelf, the seabed off its coast, without owning that seabed. Its exclusive rights to the resources there are enough for a court to order the work stopped.
grand-capri-atlantis-isle-of-gold.challenge: A federal court permanently barred construction
grand-capri-atlantis-isle-of-gold.stopped_by: US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, in 1970

minerva.story: The Republic of Minerva was an attempt in 1972 to create a new country on the Minerva Reefs, two reefs in the South Pacific between Fiji and Tonga that were submerged at high tide. Its backer was Michael Oliver, a Nevada real estate developer and coin dealer, who had published a constitution for a new country in 1968 and wanted one with no taxation, welfare or subsidies. He raised money from about 2,000 investors through a body called the Ocean Life Research Foundation. He first tried to buy an island from a government and found no seller, so the group chose to build its own land. In 1971 barges brought sand from Australia and piled it on the reefs, and a small platform and flag were added. A declaration of independence went to neighbouring states on 19 January 1972, with Morris 'Bud' Davis as provisional president. Tonga had not included the reefs in its 1887 territorial claim, and Fiji's prime minister asked what would stop such people claiming land in Fiji. At a conference on 24 February, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Nauru, Samoa and the Cook Islands backed a Tongan claim. Tonga proclaimed the reefs and the waters within 12 miles as its own on 15 June. A Tongan expedition arrived on 18 June, and the king, Taufa'ahau Tupou IV, sailed out with a convict work party and a four-piece brass band. The platform was dismantled within hours. Oliver then dismissed Davis and the project collapsed.
minerva.mechanism: Land built by hand on a reef does not become a state just because no one has yet claimed the reef. Here nearby states responded by agreeing that one of them should annex it, meaning formally add it to its territory.
minerva.recognition: None. In September 1972 the South Pacific Forum named Tonga as the only possible owner, without explicitly recognising its title
minerva.stopped_by: King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV of Tonga, who annexed the reefs
minerva.cost: About 2,000 investors backed the foundation; the total is not confirmed

minerva-1982-and-fiji-tonga.story: The Minerva Reefs are two submerged atolls, or ring-shaped coral reefs, between Fiji and Tonga, which Tonga annexed in 1972 to stop a private group founding a country there. In 1982 a group of Americans led by Morris 'Bud' Davis, the former provisional president of that Republic of Minerva, tried to occupy them again. Tongan troops forced them off after three weeks. No later group is reported to have taken possession, and Reason magazine later described the structure as more or less reclaimed by the sea. The argument then passed to the two states, because a recognised reef can give its owner rights over the surrounding waters. In 2005 Fiji declared that it did not recognise any maritime claims by Tonga based on the reefs under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the 1982 treaty on states' rights at sea. That November Fiji complained to the International Seabed Authority, the body that oversees the deep ocean floor, and Tonga lodged a counter-claim. In 2010 and again in May 2011 Fiji's navy destroyed navigation equipment on the reefs, and in June 2011 Tongan navy ships went to replace it. In July 2014 Tonga's lands minister proposed giving the reefs to Fiji in exchange for the Lau Islands. No report shows the dispute has been settled.
minerva-1982-and-fiji-tonga.mechanism: Force ended the private claim, but annexing the reef left two states arguing over what sea rights it creates. Under the law of the sea, a recognised feature can give its owner rights over the waters around it.
minerva-1982-and-fiji-tonga.challenge: Tongan troops removed the group after three weeks

new-atlantis.story: New Atlantis was a tiny republic on a raft off Jamaica, created by Leicester Hemingway, the brother of the novelist Ernest Hemingway. He built the raft of bamboo, steel, iron pipe and rock, 8 by 30 feet, had it towed about 6 to 8 miles off Bluefields, Jamaica, onto a shallow bank in waters then considered international, and anchored it with an old Ford engine block. On 4 July 1964 he declared a republic, though one profile gives 1965. He based his claim on the US Guano Islands Act of 1856, which lets American citizens claim guano-covered islands for the United States, guano being seabird droppings used as fertiliser. He gave the half of the raft where birds were encouraged to leave droppings to the United States and kept the rest as his nation. By 1965 six people were listed as inhabitants, and they unanimously elected him president. He also claimed the seafloor 50 feet below and planned to pile up rocks into an island. He wanted to pay for marine research by selling stamps, but the Universal Postal Union, the international body that coordinates mail, refused them. A State Department letter addressed to the 'Acting President' was presented as recognition. Within a few years tropical storms destroyed the raft, and local fishermen salvaged the wreckage.
new-atlantis.mechanism: The 1856 Guano Islands Act lets US citizens claim islands with guano deposits for the United States. Hemingway stretched it to cover a man-made raft, and no court tested the idea because storms destroyed the raft first.
new-atlantis.currency: The scruple, made up of items such as fish hooks, carob beans and shark teeth
new-atlantis.laws: A constitution copied almost word for word from the US Constitution
new-atlantis.challenge: No state acted before storms destroyed it
new-atlantis.recognition: None. A State Department letter to the 'Acting President' was presented as recognition, and the Universal Postal Union refused its stamps

new-utopia.story: New Utopia was a planned tax-free country on concrete platforms over the Misteriosa Bank, an underwater rise in the Caribbean about 115 miles west of the Cayman Islands. It existed only as a sales pitch. Howard Turney, who ran an anti-ageing clinic in Mexico, renamed himself Lazarus Long around 1995 after a character in Robert Heinlein's novels and promoted it. A website of more than 100 pages offered government bonds, meaning loans to the new country, at 9.5 percent interest, and promised currency returns as high as 200 percent. Plans included 642 apartments and a casino. On 8 April 1999 the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which polices investment sales, filed suit. It alleged false statements about construction, the companies involved, the safety of the investment and the SEC's own inquiry. Judge Michael Burrage in Tulsa, Oklahoma, issued an emergency order freezing the money, which the Associated Press put near $100,000 at that stage. On 20 January 2000 Long accepted a final judgment without contesting it and was barred from further violations. The SEC waived repayment of $24,000 plus interest because he swore he could not pay. The SEC says about $24,000 was raised, while encyclopedia entries claim $100 million. Long died in April 2012. His daughter announced a revival in 2017, and no later report shows anything came of it.
new-utopia.mechanism: US securities law, which governs the sale of investments, applied to internet sales aimed at US investors whatever flag or territory the offer claimed. Promising a future sovereign country gave no protection from fraud rules.
new-utopia.currency: Paper notes showing Long's face, according to the SEC
new-utopia.laws: Planned a 20% tax on imported goods
new-utopia.challenge: The SEC froze the assets in April 1999, and a consent judgment followed in January 2000
new-utopia.cost: The SEC found $24,000 raised against a $350 million bond offer; the Associated Press reported an early estimate near $100,000

operation-atlantis.story: Operation Atlantis was an effort to found a new country in the Caribbean, begun in 1968 by Werner Stiefel, head of a soap and dermatology company. Inspired by the writer Ayn Rand, he gathered followers at a motel in Saugerties, New York, and paid Spencer Heath MacCallum with a 2% share to draft a constitution. He tried to buy the Prickly Pear Cays near Anguilla for $100,000, and the sale fell through. Members then spent a year building a 38-foot concrete boat, Atlantis II, under a geodesic dome. Launched on the Hudson River in December 1971, it capsized at low tide. It later reached the Bahamas, where a storm destroyed it. Stiefel bought another ship and went to Silver Shoals, a reef area claimed by both Haiti and the Bahamas, with water four feet deep at low tide. He built sea walls and was about to dredge up sand when gunboats ordered his group to leave. Accounts differ on whether they were Haitian or Dominican. He then leased a base on Tortuga, a Haitian island, until officials read the group's newsletter and cancelled the lease. An oil rig bound for the Misteriosa Bank was destroyed by a hurricane, and the project ended. A participant says the group later bought Hatchet Caye in Belize and lived there until 2005.
operation-atlantis.mechanism: A shallow reef that two nearby states both claim offers no empty legal space. A coastal navy could remove an unarmed group without any court being involved.
operation-atlantis.currency: The deca, holding a decagram of silver, struck on a soap press
operation-atlantis.laws: A constitution drafted by Spencer Heath MacCallum in return for a 2% share
operation-atlantis.challenge: Ordered off Silver Shoals and expelled from Tortuga
operation-atlantis.stopped_by: Gunboats at Silver Shoals, hurricanes and the Haitian government
operation-atlantis.pop: A small group at a New York motel; no confirmed figure
operation-atlantis.cost: Stiefel agreed $100,000 for the Prickly Pear Cays, but the sale did not complete

condominiums-new-hebrides-andorra-brcko.story: A condominium, in international law, is a territory shared and governed by two or more powers. New Hebrides, in the South Pacific, was a French and British condominium from 1906 until it became independent in 1980 as the republic now called Vanuatu. Nauru, also in the Pacific, was run jointly by Australia, New Zealand and Britain until independence in 1968. Brčko District in Bosnia and Herzegovina, created on 8 March 2000, is held jointly by the country's two internal entities because of its mixed population, and it has 493 square kilometres and 83,516 people. Andorra, in the Pyrenees between France and Spain, was once treated in French law as a French and Spanish condominium. It is a sovereign state and is now more commonly called a co-principality, because two foreigners share its head of state by virtue of their offices, the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain. All these arrangements came from agreements between the powers concerned. Brčko remains a shared district, while New Hebrides and Nauru are now independent states.
condominiums-new-hebrides-andorra-brcko.mechanism: Two or more states can agree to govern a territory together, an arrangement known as a condominium. Such shared rule can last for decades and can lead to independence, as it did for Vanuatu and Nauru.

corpus-separatum-jerusalem.story: Corpus separatum, Latin for 'separated body', was a United Nations plan to place Jerusalem and its surroundings under international government. It was part of the UN Partition Plan for Palestine, adopted by the General Assembly on 29 November 1947 as Resolution 181, which also proposed separate Arab and Jewish states. The city was to have special status because of its importance to Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and the idea drew on the Vatican's long concern for the Christian holy places. The area ran from Abu Dis in the east to Bethlehem in the south, Ein Karim in the west and Shu'fat in the north. A governor appointed by the UN Trusteeship Council, the UN body overseeing territories not yet self-governing, would run it, and its founding law would be reviewed after ten years and put to a referendum. It was never carried out. Palestinian and other Arab leaders first rejected it, though Wikipedia says Arab governments later supported it. The British left on 14 May 1948 without setting up the regime, and the 1948 Arab-Israeli War left Israel holding the west of the city and Transjordan, now Jordan, the east. In December 1949 Israeli prime minister David Ben-Gurion declared the plan void, and the General Assembly reaffirmed it days later, but the statute approved in 1950 was never applied. In 2012 the European Parliament and the General Assembly expressed support for Jerusalem as a dual capital of Israel and a State of Palestine, with exact positions varying.
corpus-separatum-jerusalem.mechanism: A General Assembly plan is a recommendation and takes effect only if the parties on the ground accept it or someone enforces it. Here no one did, so the international city never existed.
corpus-separatum-jerusalem.stopped_by: Rejection by Arab leaders, the 1948 war and later Israeli rejection
corpus-separatum-jerusalem.recognition: Adopted by the UN General Assembly but never carried out

eastern-slavonia-untaes.story: Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Sirmium is a region along the Danube River in eastern Croatia that was run by the United Nations for two years so it could return to Croatia without more fighting. It was held by local Serbs when the Erdut Agreement of November 1995, between the Croatian government and their representatives, set up the transition. UN Security Council Resolution 1037 then created the UN Transitional Authority, known as UNTAES, on 15 January 1996. At full strength it had about 4,800 soldiers, 99 military observers and 400 police. UNTAES helped organise voting in the region for Croatia's Chamber of Counties, the upper house of parliament, on 13 April 1997. Its mission ended on 15 January 1998, and the UN says it peacefully reintegrated the territory into Croatia. The region remains part of Croatia.
eastern-slavonia-untaes.mechanism: The UN can run disputed land directly for a fixed period, with the aim of returning it to the state that claims it. The parties' own agreement gave the UN that role here.
eastern-slavonia-untaes.stopped_by: The UN mandate ended on schedule in January 1998
eastern-slavonia-untaes.laws: The Erdut Agreement and UN Security Council Resolution 1037
eastern-slavonia-untaes.recognition: UN administration of land recognised as Croatian

free-city-of-danzig.story: The Free City of Danzig was a small self-governing state on the Baltic coast, centred on the port now called Gdańsk in Poland. It existed from 1920 to 1939. After the First World War, US President Woodrow Wilson's peace plan promised newly independent Poland secure access to the sea, which suggested giving it the port. About 90% of Danzig's people were German, though, so the Allies compromised in Article 100 of the Treaty of Versailles. The city and nearly 200 smaller places became a city-state of 1,952 square kilometres, with 366,730 people in 1923, under the protection of the League of Nations, the international body of the time. A League High Commissioner oversaw it. It had its own parliament, the Volkstag, and from 1923 its own currency, the gulden. Poland handled its foreign relations and defence, shared a customs union with it and ran its railways and post, and had rights at the port. To reduce its dependence on Danzig, Poland began building a rival port at Gdynia in 1921, whose trade passed Danzig's by 1933. The Nazi Party won about 50% of the Volkstag vote on 28 May 1933 and took over the city's government, the Senate, that June. On 1 September 1939 Germany attacked Poland, firing on the Polish depot at Westerplatte in Danzig harbour, and the city was annexed the same day. The Red Army took it in March 1945, it went to Poland, and most of its German residents were expelled or left.
free-city-of-danzig.mechanism: A city-state protected by an international body depends on that body being willing and able to defend it. The League of Nations guarantee did not stop Germany annexing Danzig in 1939.
free-city-of-danzig.laws: Its own constitution and parliament (the Volkstag), overseen by the League of Nations
free-city-of-danzig.recognition: Created by treaty under League of Nations protection

free-territory-of-trieste.story: The Free Territory of Trieste was meant to be a neutral independent country on the Adriatic Sea between Italy and Yugoslavia, under the direct responsibility of the UN Security Council. Both Italy and Yugoslavia wanted the port, which had a mixed population, and the plan was intended to end their rival claims after the Second World War. It was created by the Treaty of Peace with Italy of 10 February 1947 and came into existence on 15 September 1947. The treaty and a UN resolution required a governor, but the Security Council never appointed one, so it never worked as an independent state, though its formal status was generally respected. Instead it stayed split in two. Zone A, the city and coast, was under Allied military rule, and Zone B was under Yugoslav rule, each with its own version of the lira. On 5 October 1954 the United States, Britain, Italy and Yugoslavia signed the London Memorandum, which ended Allied rule in Zone A. Italy took Zone A and Yugoslavia kept Zone B. The Treaty of Osimo, signed in 1975 and in force from 1977, settled the border between them, so the territory no longer exists.
free-territory-of-trieste.mechanism: A state created on paper by treaty and the UN cannot function if the officials it requires are never appointed. Trieste's governor never was, so the two occupying powers kept running it until they divided it.
free-territory-of-trieste.stopped_by: The London Memorandum of 1954, which divided it between Italy and Yugoslavia

memel-klaipeda.story: The Memel Territory, now the Klaipėda Region of Lithuania, was a strip of 2,657 square kilometres on the Baltic coast that passed through several hands between the world wars. Under Article 99 of the Treaty of Versailles, Germany gave it up in favour of the victorious Allies, who said its port was the only sea outlet for newly independent Lithuania. They did not hand it over, though. It was run for them under the Conference of Ambassadors, by the French general Dominique Odry from February 1920 and then by High Commissioner Gabriel Petisné from May 1921, with French troops present. In January 1923 Lithuanian militias, mainly from Lithuania itself, staged the Klaipėda Revolt and occupied the territory. The French garrison, with France occupied elsewhere in the Ruhr, did little to stop them, and Lithuania annexed it. A convention of 8 May 1924 confirmed the annexation and gave the region its own parliament and two official languages. A Lithuanian census in 1925 counted 141,000 people, with German the largest language group. On 23 March 1939, after an oral German ultimatum, Lithuania's foreign minister Juozas Urbšys and his German counterpart Joachim von Ribbentrop signed a treaty handing the territory to Germany. After 1945 the Soviet Union made it part of Soviet Lithuania, and most remaining Germans were expelled or later left. It stayed part of Lithuania when the country regained independence in 1990.
memel-klaipeda.mechanism: A treaty can take land from one state without settling who gets it next. Here that left it open to seizure by a neighbour, whose title the Allies then accepted, and later to loss under threat from a stronger state.
memel-klaipeda.stopped_by: Lithuanian takeover in 1923, then a German ultimatum in 1939
memel-klaipeda.challenge: A revolt in January 1923 and a German ultimatum in March 1939
memel-klaipeda.recognition: Run for the Allies, then annexed by Lithuania, which a 1924 convention confirmed

saar-basin-1920-1935.story: The Territory of the Saar Basin was a coal-mining region on the border of Germany and France, taken out of German government for 15 years by the Treaty of Versailles after the First World War. Under Article 45 Germany gave the coal mines to France as compensation for mines destroyed in northern France. Under Article 49 Germany gave up governing the territory in favour of the League of Nations, the international body of the time, which held it as a trustee until residents voted on its future after 15 years. A five-member Governing Commission ruled from 1920 and alone made the law, and a 30-member regional council formed in 1922 could only advise. The territory had the Saar franc, its own postage stamps and 812,000 people in 1933. In the vote of 13 January 1935, on a 98% turnout, 90.8% chose to rejoin Germany, 8.8% to keep the existing status and 0.4% to join France. The territory ended on 1 March 1935 and returned to Germany. After the Second World War the Saar was again separated, as a French-controlled protectorate from 1947 to 1956. A referendum on 23 October 1955 ended French rule, and the Saarland joined West Germany on 1 January 1957. It remains a German state.
saar-basin-1920-1935.mechanism: A treaty can suspend a state's government over land for a fixed term and hand the final choice to the residents. The Saar's 1935 vote carried that out, returning it to Germany.
saar-basin-1920-1935.stopped_by: The 1935 plebiscite (a public vote), in which residents chose Germany
saar-basin-1920-1935.recognition: Held in trust by the League of Nations

tangier-international-zone.story: The Tangier International Zone was an area of 373 square kilometres around the Moroccan port of Tangier, on the Strait of Gibraltar, run jointly by foreign powers. France and Spain both wanted the city, and Britain wanted it neutral to protect its position in the strait. France, Spain and Britain settled this by a convention signed in Paris on 18 December 1923, and the zone began on 1 June 1925. Italy joined on equal terms in 1928. An appointed International Legislative Assembly made laws, supervised by a Committee of Control made up of the consuls of Belgium, France, Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain. An Administrator held executive power, and a representative of Morocco's Sultan, the Mendoub, had authority over the Muslim and Jewish communities. A Mixed Court, with judges appointed by Belgium, Britain, Spain, France and Italy, replaced the separate courts each foreign power had run. Spanish troops occupied the city in June 1940 and Spain held it until October 1945, when the international system was restored. The zone had no tariffs, exchange controls or income taxes, and it became a banking centre, with 85 banks by 1950. It also became known for tolerance and drew writers and gay men from Western countries, many of whom could live openly there. After France and Spain ended their rule over Morocco in 1956, a protocol signed in Tangier on 29 October 1956 returned the zone to full Moroccan sovereignty.
tangier-international-zone.mechanism: Foreign states can run a territory jointly by agreement among themselves, without making it their own. The arrangement ended when the local state regained full independence and took the territory back by agreement.
tangier-international-zone.stopped_by: Moroccan independence; a protocol of 29 October 1956 returned the zone to Morocco
tangier-international-zone.laws: An International Legislative Assembly and a Mixed Court of foreign judges
tangier-international-zone.recognition: Run jointly by the powers that signed the treaty
tangier-international-zone.why: Entry said the powers agreed at Rabat in July 1952 to abolish the zone. The dedicated article says a revised status was negotiated in 1952 and the zone ended by protocol on 29 October 1956, so the 1952 claim was removed.

abkhazia.story: Abkhazia is a breakaway territory of about 8,665 square kilometres on the Black Sea coast, in the north-west of Georgia and bordering Russia. It governs itself from the city of Sukhumi, but most of the world treats it as part of Georgia. In July 1992 its Abkhaz leaders declared effective independence, and that August Georgia's National Guard entered, starting a war. Abkhaz forces took Sukhumi in September 1993. Up to 250,000 ethnic Georgians were driven out and about 5,000 killed, and summits of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), a body of European and other states, recognised this as ethnic cleansing. A ceasefire followed in 1994, and in October 1999 Abkhazia passed a formal act of independence. During the Russo-Georgian War of August 2008 about 9,000 Russian soldiers entered, and on 26 August Russia recognised its independence. Georgia calls it a Russian-occupied territory. Russia supplies about half of its budget, its rouble is the currency in practice, and most residents hold Russian passports, because Abkhazian ones cannot be used for international travel. Four UN members recognise it (Russia, Syria, Nicaragua and Venezuela), along with South Ossetia and Transnistria, two other unrecognised states. Tuvalu, Vanuatu and Nauru recognised it and later withdrew. After Assad fell in Syria in December 2024, the Georgian fact-checker Myth Detector found no official withdrawal as of July 2025. About 244,000 people lived there in 2025, and it is not a UN member.
abkhazia.mechanism: Holding land and running a government can make a territory independent in practice. It stays outside the United Nations without wider recognition from other states, and small states can withdraw recognition later.
abkhazia.laws: Its own government and laws, with close treaty ties to Russia
abkhazia.recognition: Russia, Syria, Nicaragua, Venezuela, South Ossetia and Transnistria; three others withdrew

biafra-1967.story: Biafra was a breakaway republic in south-eastern Nigeria that existed from 1967 to 1970. It covered Nigeria's former Eastern Region and had about 13.5 million people, mainly Igbo with sizeable Ijaw, Efik, Ibibio and other populations. After ethnic tension, military coups and a 1966 pogrom against Igbo people, the region's governor, Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu, declared independence on 30 May 1967. Nigeria's military moved to retake the territory, which started the Nigerian Civil War. Five states recognised Biafra officially, Gabon, Haiti, Côte d'Ivoire, Tanzania and Zambia. France, Portugal, Israel, South Africa and Rhodesia treated it as a state in practice and gave covert military support. Biafra also issued its own pound. Wikipedia reports that around two million Biafran civilians died in nearly three years of war. Ojukwu fled to Côte d'Ivoire, Philip Effiong oversaw the surrender, and the territory rejoined Nigeria on 15 January 1970. It remains part of Nigeria, and Igbo nationalism has grown more militant since the 1990s.
biafra-1967.mechanism: Recognition by other states does not protect a breakaway state that cannot hold its land. Five states recognised Biafra, and it still ended when it lost the war against Nigeria.
biafra-1967.stopped_by: The Nigerian military; Biafra surrendered on 15 January 1970
biafra-1967.challenge: It lost the Nigerian Civil War

bougainville-2019.story: Bougainville is an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea in the South Pacific that voted for independence in 2019 and is still waiting for it. It was made a province in 1976 after Papua New Guinea became independent. A civil war from 1988 to 1998 ended with a 2001 peace agreement that promised a referendum. The vote ran from 23 November to 7 December 2019 and offered a choice of greater autonomy or independence. Independence won 176,928 votes to 3,043, or 98.31%, with turnout of 87.38%, though press and parliamentary reports in 2026 give the share as 97.7%. The vote was not binding, and Papua New Guinea's national parliament has the final decision. In July 2021 the two governments agreed that Bougainville would become independent by 2027, subject to that parliament's approval. In July 2026 a forum of Bougainville leaders recommended 1 September 2030 as the target date. The result was tabled in parliament on 27 August 2026, and Prime Minister James Marape said the two governments would consult in October to set a date for the vote. Minister Manasseh Makiba said a yes vote would start a transitional phase of self-government and would not bring immediate independence. The majority required is disputed. The national government says two-thirds or three-quarters of an absolute majority, the governing coalition has asked for 89 MPs, and the Bougainville government argues for 60 seats. AAP, an Australian news agency, reports that Bougainville's government plans to declare sovereignty by 2030 if parliament delays further. No report by November 2026 gives a date for the vote.
bougainville-2019.mechanism: A peace agreement can promise a vote without promising the outcome. Bougainville's agreement left the final decision with the parliament of the state it wants to leave.
bougainville-2019.recognition: Not independent; the vote is accepted as held, and the decision awaits Papua New Guinea's parliament

catalonia-2017.story: Catalonia is a region of north-eastern Spain with its own parliament and government, which in 2017 tried to become independent through a referendum that Spain's courts had blocked. The Catalan parliament, with a pro-independence majority under President Carles Puigdemont, approved a referendum law on 6 September 2017, while 52 opposing members boycotted the vote. The next day Spain's Constitutional Court, which rules on whether laws fit the constitution, suspended the law at the request of the Spanish government, which called it a breach of the constitution. The vote went ahead on 1 October, and National Police and Civil Guard officers used force at polling stations. Yes took 2,044,038 votes, or 90.18%, on a turnout of 43.03%. The Catalan government estimated that up to 770,000 votes could not be cast because of the police action, and observers it had invited said the vote fell short of international standards. The court declared the law void on 17 October. On 27 October the Catalan parliament declared independence, and the same day Spain's Senate voted 214 to 47 to use Article 155 of the constitution, which let the national government take direct control of some Catalan powers. No state recognised the declaration. In the 2024 Catalan elections independence parties lost control of the regional government, and an amnesty was passed that year for crimes linked to the referendum. Catalonia remains part of Spain.
catalonia-2017.mechanism: A region's vote held against a constitutional court's order has no legal effect within the state. Spain's constitution also let the national government take direct control of the region in response.
catalonia-2017.stopped_by: Spain's Constitutional Court and Article 155 of the Spanish constitution
catalonia-2017.challenge: Spain's Constitutional Court voided the referendum law, and Spain took direct control
catalonia-2017.recognition: None; no state recognised the result

compacts-of-free-association.story: The Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau are three independent countries in the western Pacific that have a special treaty relationship with the United States, called free association. All three were part of the US-run Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, a UN arrangement meant to lead to self-government or independence. Each chose to become a sovereign state, meaning a self-governing country in law, while keeping close ties to the United States. Referendums in 1983 and 1984 came before the treaties, known as compacts. These took effect on 21 October 1986 for the Marshall Islands, 3 November 1986 for Micronesia and 1 October 1994 for Palau, whose agreement was signed in 1986 and took eight more years to come into force. Under the compacts the United States pays guaranteed financial assistance and gives access to some US services. In return it holds full authority over their defence. The agreements have no end date, though the economic terms are renewed from time to time, most recently for 2024 to 2043 under US Public Law 118-42. All three remain independent and in association with the United States.
compacts-of-free-association.mechanism: A territory can become a sovereign state while handing defence to a larger state by treaty in return for funding. The arrangement is known as free association.
compacts-of-free-association.recognition: Sovereign states in free association with the United States

eritrea-1993.story: Eritrea is a country on the Red Sea in the Horn of Africa that won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, after a long war and a vote observed by the United Nations. It had been an Italian colony from 1890 and came under British administration after the Second World War. In 1950 the UN voted to join it to Ethiopia in a federation with some self-rule. By 1962 Ethiopia's Emperor Haile Selassie had ended that self-rule and made Eritrea a province, and an armed rebellion followed. The war ended in May 1991, when the Eritrean People's Liberation Front, the main rebel movement, defeated Ethiopian forces. The Front had first proposed a referendum in 1981. Transitional governments planned the vote, and a UN mission called UNOVER, set up by the General Assembly in December 1992, observed and checked it. Voting ran from 23 to 25 April 1993, and 99.83% chose independence, 1,100,260 votes against 1,822. Reports of turnout range from 93.93% to above 98%. Independence was declared on 27 April 1993, and Eritrea joined the UN on 28 May.
eritrea-1993.mechanism: Winning a war gave the Eritrean movement control, and a UN-checked vote then gave other states grounds to accept the result. The combination produced a recognised state.
eritrea-1993.recognition: An independent state, with the result recognised; UN member since 28 May 1993

independence-referendum-record.story: An independence referendum is a public vote in which residents decide whether their territory should become a separate country. A Yes vote does not always bring independence. Wikipedia's table, as retrieved in November 2026, lists about 123 such votes since Chile in 1817. Counting its outcomes gives 59 votes ending in a No, 31 in a Yes followed by independence and recognition from other states, 16 in a Yes with no independence, and 12 in a Yes where the territory took control on the ground without general recognition. The rest ended in a status linked to another state, a disputed independence or continuing negotiation. Western Australia voted Yes in 1933 and stayed in Australia. Nevis, in the Caribbean, voted Yes in 1998 and fell short of the two-thirds majority required. Quebec voted No in 1980 and 1995. Iraqi Kurdistan voted Yes in 2005 and 2017 without result. Votes held on terms agreed with the state being left can be binding and accepted abroad. Votes held without its consent can lead to one-sided declarations of independence and states that only some countries recognise.
independence-referendum-record.mechanism: A referendum carries real weight when its terms were agreed with the state being left. A Yes vote without that agreement rarely brings recognition from other states.

katanga-1960.story: The State of Katanga was a breakaway republic in the mining south of Congo, in central Africa, from 1960 to 1963. Congo became independent from Belgium on 30 June 1960. Eleven days later Moïse Tshombe, leader of the local CONAKAT party, declared Katanga independent, saying the central government under Patrice Lumumba was dictatorial and leaned towards communism. Its capital was Élisabethville, now Lubumbashi, and it covered 496,871 square kilometres with about 1.7 million people. Money and foreign help kept it going. Union Minière du Haut-Katanga, a mining company with exclusive copper rights there since 1906, advanced Tshombe 1,250 million Belgian francs, about US$25 million, and GlobalSecurity reports that Katanga supplied 10% of the world's copper and 60% of its cobalt that year. In September 1960 about 1,133 Belgian technicians and 231 Belgian officers and non-commissioned officers were attached to the government, and in early 1961 nearly 500 British, Rhodesian, French and South African irregular fighters arrived. Wikipedia says Belgium gave recognition in practice on 16 July 1960, while GlobalSecurity says Belgium never officially recognised it but gave military, economic and technical help. The United States refused. Lumumba asked the UN for military help, and in February 1961 the Security Council authorised force as a last resort to prevent civil war. UN Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld died in a plane crash during peace talks that year. UN forces launched Operation Grandslam on 28 December 1962 and held Élisabethville within three days. Tshombe conceded in January 1963, UN officials entered his last stronghold, Kolwezi, on 21 January, and Katanga rejoined Congo as a province.
katanga-1960.mechanism: A mining company's money and a region's revenue can fund a breakaway government for a time. Whether it lasts depends on outside recognition and force, and here UN troops ended it.
katanga-1960.recognition: Never gained general recognition; sources differ on whether Belgium recognised it
katanga-1960.challenge: Opposed by the Congo government and UN forces

kosovo-2008.story: Kosovo is a territory in the Balkans, in south-eastern Europe, that declared independence from Serbia in 2008 and is recognised by more than half of UN members. It had been an autonomous province within Serbia, then part of Yugoslavia. In 1990 its assembly voted to declare independence, and only Albania recognised that. After the Kosovo War, UN Security Council Resolution 1244 placed it under a UN mission from 1999, with a NATO-led force providing security. Before and during the handover an estimated 100,000 Serbs and other non-Albanians fled. On 17 February 2008, 109 of the 120 assembly members adopted a new declaration of independence. Serbia called it illegal and that year persuaded the UN General Assembly, by 77 votes to 6 with 74 abstentions, to ask the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, for an opinion. On 22 July 2010 the court ruled 10 to 4 that the declaration did not violate international law. Talks led to a deal between Belgrade and Pristina in Brussels in 2013. Kosovo is recognised by 110 UN members, Taiwan, the Cook Islands and Niue, and 8 other UN members have withdrawn recognition. It belongs to the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, but it is not a UN member.
kosovo-2008.mechanism: The International Court of Justice said in 2010 that declaring independence does not in itself break international law. Membership of the United Nations still depends on the votes of other states.
kosovo-2008.laws: Under a UN mission from 1999, then its own institutions
kosovo-2008.challenge: Serbia took it to the International Court of Justice, which found no violation of international law
kosovo-2008.recognition: 110 UN members, Taiwan, the Cook Islands and Niue; 8 withdrew; not a UN member

montenegro-2006.story: Montenegro, a small country on the Adriatic coast in south-eastern Europe, left its union with Serbia in 2006 by using a right written into the union's own constitution. Article 60 of the 2003 Constitutional Charter of Serbia and Montenegro allowed a member to leave after at least three years, by referendum. The Montenegrin government wanted a simple majority to be enough, and the opposition insisted on a higher bar, so a disputed rule requiring 55% was adopted. On 21 May 2006 Yes won 55.5% on a turnout of 86.49%, 230,711 votes against 184,954, narrowly clearing it. An earlier vote in 1992 had gone against independence. All five permanent members of the UN Security Council accepted the preliminary result by 23 May, and the United States, China, Russia and the European Union said they would respect it. Parliament formally declared independence on 3 June, which dissolved the union, and Serbia declared itself the union's legal successor, meaning it took over its treaties and memberships. Montenegro joined the UN on 28 June 2006.
montenegro-2006.mechanism: When a union's constitution contains an exit clause, a member has a clear legal way to leave. Because Montenegro used it, outside powers accepted the result within days.
montenegro-2006.laws: Article 60 of the Constitutional Charter of Serbia and Montenegro
montenegro-2006.recognition: An independent state; all five permanent Security Council members accepted the result; UN member since 28 June 2006

new-caledonia-kanaky-referendums.story: New Caledonia is a French territory in the South Pacific, known as Kanaky to many of its Indigenous Kanak people, whose future has been argued over through three referendums and years of talks. The Matignon Agreements of 1988 and the Nouméa Accord of 1998, signed by France and the main parties on both sides, set a 20-year transition and allowed up to three votes on independence. Voters rejected independence by 57% in 2018 and 53% in 2020. The third vote was set for 12 December 2021. Kanak leaders asked for a delay after a COVID-19 outbreak that caused 280 deaths, saying mourning rituals could last a year. Opponents replied that the outbreak had declined by mid-November and accused them of using it as an excuse. The vote went ahead under a Kanak boycott, and No took 96.5% on a turnout of 43.87%. Riots in May 2024 over plans to open the frozen voter rolls, which would let more French nationals vote, killed 14 people and caused over €2 billion in damage. The Bougival accord of July 2025 and the Élysée-Oudinot accord of January 2026 proposed a new status. The FLNKS, the main pro-independence alliance, withdrew from Bougival, saying it had been misled, and boycotted the talks. On 2 April 2026 France's National Assembly rejected the constitutional bill without debate, 190 to 107. Delayed provincial elections on 28 June 2026 gave pro-independence parties 26 of 54 Congress seats, the pro-France bloc 24 and the party Éveil Océanien 4. In July 2026 Congress elected the pro-France Virginie Ruffenach as president. Its long-term status remains under talks with France, with no date set.
new-caledonia-kanaky-referendums.mechanism: An agreed series of votes can run its full course and still leave the question open. Because one side boycotted New Caledonia's last vote, it did not accept the result as settling the matter.
new-caledonia-kanaky-referendums.recognition: French territory; independence rejected in three votes, the last of them boycotted

puntland.story: Puntland is a self-governing state in north-east Somalia, on the Horn of Africa, with its capital at Garowe. Somalia's civil war began in 1991, the year its ruler Siad Barre fell. In 1998 local politicians, elders, business people and civil groups held a three-month conference in Garowe, and on 1 August they founded Puntland to provide services, security and trade. It was set up as a homeland for the Harti clan group, with the Majeerteen clan as its chief architects. It covers 212,510 square kilometres, and its 2016 population estimate was 4,334,633. It has its own constitution, adopted at a convention in April 2012. Unlike Somaliland, its neighbour to the west, which claims to be a separate country, Puntland has held that it is part of Somalia, and it disputes the Sool, Sanaag and Ayn regions with Somaliland. On 31 March 2024, during a dispute over Somalia's constitution, Puntland said it no longer recognised the federal government, would stop taking part in federal institutions, and would exercise the powers of an independent state until a federal constitution is approved in a referendum it takes part in. No report shows any foreign government recognising it as a separate state.
puntland.mechanism: A region can run its own government and suspend ties with the centre while still saying it belongs to the state. Puntland has done this since 2024 without claiming to be a separate country in law.
puntland.laws: Its own constitution, adopted in April 2012
puntland.challenge: Withdrew recognition of Somalia's federal government on 31 March 2024
puntland.recognition: A federal member state of Somalia, and it counts itself part of Somalia

republic-of-new-afrika.story: The Republic of New Afrika is a Black nationalist organisation in the United States that seeks an independent country in the Black Belt of the American South. It also demands reparations from the US government for slavery and the Jim Crow segregation laws, and a vote of African Americans on their citizenship. The Malcolm X Society, a Detroit group, called a Black Government Conference in Detroit on 31 March 1968, attended by about 500 people. It adopted a declaration of independence, a constitution and a provisional government. Robert F. Williams, then in exile in Cuba, was chosen as first president, with Gaidi Obadele (Milton Henry) and Betty Shabazz, the widow of Malcolm X, as vice presidents. The group claimed Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina as 'subjugated national territory' and announced a capital on a member's farm in Hinds County, Mississippi. Shootouts followed at New Bethel Baptist Church in Detroit in 1969 and in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1971, in which law-enforcement officers were killed and injured. Members were prosecuted and said they acted in self-defence. The organisation declined in the early 1970s, which Wikipedia attributes mainly to government raids and mass arrests that jailed its leaders. Chokwe Lumumba, elected a vice president in 1971, became a lawyer and was mayor of Jackson from 2013 until his death in 2014. The group still lists officers, though no report describes current activity.
republic-of-new-afrika.mechanism: A provisional government that claims land by declaration, without the agreement of the state that holds it, gains no territory in law. Here the state answered with raids and prosecutions.
republic-of-new-afrika.stopped_by: Federal and state raids and arrests

sahrawi-republic.story: The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic is a government in exile for Western Sahara, a desert territory on the Atlantic coast of north-west Africa, most of which Morocco holds. It was the Spanish colony of Spanish Sahara until 1975, when Spain left and handed administration to Morocco and Mauritania under the Madrid Accords. The Polisario Front, a movement seeking an independent state for the Sahrawi people, proclaimed the republic on 27 February 1976 at Bir Lehlou. Mauritania withdrew in 1979, and Morocco built a 2,700-kilometre sand wall dividing the territory. The republic claims 266,000 square kilometres and controls about 90,000 east of the wall, a share given as anywhere from a fifth to 30%. A UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991 promised a referendum, which never took place because the two sides dispute who may vote. Polisario declared the ceasefire over in November 2020. Its official capital, Laayoune, is held by Morocco, and daily government runs from the Rabuni refugee camp in Tindouf, Algeria, where about 173,600 people lived in 2023. It is a full member of the African Union. Counts of recognition range from 33 to 46 UN members, and many others have withdrawn or suspended it. The United States recognised Moroccan sovereignty in December 2020. On 31 October 2025 the Security Council voted 11 in favour, for talks based on Morocco's autonomy plan. Polisario said the resolution does not imply recognition of Moroccan rule and that it will not join talks aimed at legitimising it. In 2026 Mali said it was withdrawing recognition. The UN still lists Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory, one whose people have not yet governed themselves.
sahrawi-republic.mechanism: Membership of a regional body and dozens of recognitions from other states can give a government international standing. They have not given this one control of most of the land it claims.
sahrawi-republic.currency: Sahrawi peseta on paper; the Moroccan dirham, Algerian dinar, Mauritanian ouguiya and euro are used in practice
