sahrawi-republic.challenge: Morocco holds most of the territory
sahrawi-republic.recognition: African Union member; counts of recognition range from 33 to 46 UN members
sahrawi-republic.why: Entry said 90,000 square kilometres was 'the easternmost fifth', but that figure is about a third of 266,000; sources give different shares, and this is now stated plainly.

scotland-2014.story: Scotland, a nation within the United Kingdom, held a referendum on independence on 18 September 2014 with the agreement of the UK government. The Scottish National Party, which wants independence, won a majority in the Scottish Parliament in 2011 after promising a vote. The Scottish and UK governments negotiated until October 2012, when they reached the Edinburgh Agreement. It temporarily gave the Scottish Parliament the legal power to hold the referendum, since that power otherwise lies with the UK Parliament. Voters were asked 'Should Scotland be an independent country?', and the voting age was lowered from 18 to 16 for the occasion. The main campaigns were Yes Scotland and Better Together. No won with 2,001,926 votes, or 55.3%, against 1,617,989, or 44.7%, and turnout of 84.6% was the highest for any UK election or referendum since January 1910. After the 2016 vote to leave the European Union, in which 62% of Scottish voters chose to remain, the party called for a repeat vote. On 23 November 2022 the UK Supreme Court ruled that the Scottish Parliament cannot hold one on its own. The UK government has refused to transfer the power again, most recently after the Scottish Parliament asked for it in May 2026 and the Scottish Government published a draft bill that August. Scotland remains part of the United Kingdom.
scotland-2014.mechanism: When the parent state agrees to a vote, its result is lawful and accepted by both sides. The UK Supreme Court ruled in 2022 that Scotland cannot hold another without that agreement.

add_sources.t: Proposed second Scottish independence referendum, Wikipedia

south-ossetia.story: South Ossetia is a breakaway territory of about 3,900 square kilometres in the Caucasus Mountains, between Georgia and Russia, with its capital at Tskhinvali. Most of the world treats it as part of Georgia, and about 53,500 people lived there at a 2015 census, mostly Ossetians, a separate ethnic group from Georgians. Under the Soviet Union it was an autonomous region of Georgia. It proclaimed a republic in 1990, and Georgia abolished its autonomy that December. Georgian troops entered Tskhinvali in January 1991, and in the war that followed, with Russia backing the Ossetians, about 100,000 Ossetians and 23,000 Georgians fled their homes. A referendum on 19 January 1992 approved independence and joining Russia, and it declared independence on 29 May 1992. A second referendum in 2006 reported 99% support, and neither vote brought international recognition. War broke out with Georgia in August 2008, Russia invaded and took Tskhinvali, and on 26 August Russia recognised South Ossetia. An EU-sponsored inquiry later said open fighting began with a large Georgian military operation. Georgia calls it occupied territory, and Russia keeps a military base there with thousands of troops. Four UN members recognise it (Russia, Syria, Nicaragua and Venezuela), along with Abkhazia and Transnistria. Tuvalu and Nauru recognised it and later withdrew. A 2022 plan for a referendum on joining Russia was suspended by a new president. Marat Kambolov has been acting president since June 2026.
south-ossetia.mechanism: Repeated Yes votes held without the parent state's agreement did not bring wider recognition. Recognition came mainly from Russia, whose troops hold the territory.
south-ossetia.recognition: Russia, Syria, Nicaragua, Venezuela, Abkhazia and Transnistria; two others withdrew

south-sudan-2011.story: South Sudan, in east-central Africa, became an independent country on 9 July 2011 after voting to leave Sudan. The vote came from the 2005 Naivasha Agreement, also called the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, between the central government in Khartoum and the Sudan People's Liberation Army/Movement, the southern rebel movement. It ended the long war between north and south and fixed the terms and date of a referendum in advance. For the result to count, turnout had to reach 60%, and a simple majority would then mean separation. Preparing it needed a census, delayed three times, and voter registration, with unmapped minefields in the south, up to 5 million nomadic Sudanese, and up to 2 million displaced southerners in camps around Khartoum. Voting ran from 9 to 15 January 2011. Final results, published on 7 February, showed 98.83% for separation on a turnout of 97.58%. Wikipedia reports that ballots were suspended in 10 of 79 counties for exceeding 100% turnout, which still left the result well above the 60% needed. A parallel vote on whether Abyei, a disputed border area, would join the south was postponed over arguments about borders and who could vote, and it has been put off indefinitely. South Sudan joined the UN on 14 July 2011.
south-sudan-2011.mechanism: A separation agreed in a peace deal with the parent state, with a date fixed in advance, leads to accepted independence. Sudan had agreed to the vote, and the result was accepted.
south-sudan-2011.laws: The 2005 Naivasha Agreement set the process
south-sudan-2011.recognition: An independent state, with the result recognised; UN member since 14 July 2011

timor-leste-1999-2002.story: Timor-Leste, also called East Timor, is a country on the eastern half of the island of Timor in South-East Asia that became independent in 2002 after a UN-run vote ended Indonesian rule. Portugal was its colonial ruler. In 1975 the independence party Fretilin declared independence, and Indonesia invaded that December and annexed the territory the following year. The UN did not recognise the annexation. On 27 January 1999 Indonesian president B. J. Habibie agreed to let voters choose between special autonomy within Indonesia and independence, and a 5 May agreement between Indonesia and Portugal set the terms. On 30 August 1999, under a UN mission, 78.5% of voters rejected autonomy, on a turnout of 98.93%. Militias favouring Indonesia carried out mass violence and destruction afterwards, and a UN-backed inquiry later held the Indonesian army and militias responsible for widespread killing and forced displacement. On 15 September the UN Security Council approved a multinational force led by Australia, INTERFET, to restore order. Indonesia's assembly repealed its 1978 annexation resolution, and the UN Transitional Administration in East Timor (UNTAET) governed the territory until independence on 20 May 2002. It joined the UN that September. Many Indonesians, including the government, call the vote a consultation.
timor-leste-1999-2002.mechanism: An occupation the UN never accepted can end when the occupying state agrees to a vote. In this case the UN then ran the territory itself until it could become independent.
timor-leste-1999-2002.laws: Run by the UN Transitional Administration (UNTAET) until 2002
timor-leste-1999-2002.recognition: An independent state from 20 May 2002; UN member since 27 September 2002
timor-leste-1999-2002.why: Entry said Habibie asked the UN to hold the vote; the source says he agreed to let voters choose, with terms set by an Indonesia-Portugal agreement of 5 May 1999.

blueseed.story: Blueseed was a company in Palo Alto, California, founded on 31 July 2011 by Max Marty, Dario Mutabdzija and Dan Dascalescu, that planned to house startup founders on a ship anchored 12 nautical miles off the California coast near Silicon Valley. That spot lies just outside the US territorial sea, the belt of water a state fully controls, in the contiguous zone, where a coastal state has only limited powers. The point was to get around US immigration law. Foreign entrepreneurs could work on the ship without an H-1B work visa and travel to the mainland on easier business or tourist visas. The project received wide press coverage and a promise of investment from Peter Thiel, the technology investor, who did not invest in the seed round, the first stage of funding. It reported US$300,000 in seed funding, some Bitcoin investments and $9 million from an undisclosed investor, and said it would lease a ship. Its launch date moved from the third quarter of 2013 to late 2014, on the assumption that $18 million more would come in. The money did not arrive, and the project went on hold in 2013. Wikipedia says the company resumed in 2020 as a business accelerator, a programme that helps new firms, and dropped the ship.
blueseed.mechanism: A ship just beyond the 12-mile limit lies outside a state's full control, so work done on board might not need a work visa. The idea was never tested because the ship was never leased.
blueseed.challenge: Not tested, because no ship was leased

freedom-ship.story: Freedom Ship is a floating city proposed in the late 1990s by the engineer Norman Nixon, meant to be a mobile colony free of the property, local and national laws of any state. The plan was a chain of linked barges 1,800 metres long and 250 metres wide, with 25 floors and homes for about 80,000 people, plus a hospital, schools, a hotel, a casino and duty-free shops. It would constantly circle the globe, stopping at ports. For comparison, the largest ship ever built, the Seawise Giant, was about a quarter of that length. The company, Freedom Ship International, estimated the cost at US$6 billion in 1999 and US$11 billion by 2002. A press release in July 2008 explained how hard it was to find reliable funding. In November 2013 the company said the project was being revived at US$10 billion, with construction not yet begun, and in 2016 it was linked to Kanethara Marine in India. By 2026 estimates had reached US$15 billion and then US$20 billion. In June 2026 Euronews reported a redesign by the Florida-based Freedom Cruise Line International, led by Roger Gooch, expected to use nuclear fuel and to be built in Indonesia once funded. No launch date has been given, and no ship has been built.
freedom-ship.mechanism: The idea behind Freedom Ship is that a constantly moving vessel escapes tax and property law. That idea remains untested because the ship was never financed, and any ship would still need a flag state, the country whose law applies on board.
freedom-ship.pop: No one, because it was not built

life-at-sea.story: Life at Sea Cruises was a company, with Miray Cruises as its parent, that sold a three-year round-the-world voyage in which passengers would live aboard at prices it said rivalled ordinary living costs. It made no claim of sovereignty, but it shows what buyers risked when they paid a private company for a home at sea before any ship existed. The voyage was due to leave Istanbul, Turkey, on 1 November 2023. Shortly before that, the date moved to 11 November and the port to Amsterdam, and then to 30 November. On 17 November passengers were told the cruise was off, and the company admitted it had no ship. Some of the buyers of the 111 cabins sold were already in Istanbul, and others said they had sold or let their homes and given away their possessions. Most had spent tens of thousands of dollars. The company promised repayment in monthly instalments from mid-December to late February, and offered to pay for flights home and hotels until 1 December. By January 2024 only four passengers had received refunds, and 78 customers asked the US attorney in southern Florida, the federal prosecutor there, to open a criminal investigation over about $16 million in deposits. No report says how that request ended.
life-at-sea.mechanism: A contract to live on a ship is an ordinary consumer contract under national law. Buyers' protection depends on the company being able to pay and on courts on land.
life-at-sea.challenge: Not tested, because it never sailed

ms-satoshi.story: MS Satoshi was a 1991 cruise ship that the company Ocean Builders, led by chief executive Grant Romundt, bought in 2020 to turn into a floating community in the Gulf of Panama. The ship had sailed for P&O as the Pacific Dawn. Ocean Builders announced the plan in early October and took delivery on 5 November. It would be anchored full-time, with cabins auctioned as homes for entrepreneurs, digital nomads and cryptocurrency companies, and first residents expected as early as January 2021. Romundt then told investors the project could not go on, because no protection and indemnity insurer would cover it. That is the liability cover a ship's owners need against claims at sea. Without it there could be no crew, which meant losing the ship's class rating, the safety certificate from a ship inspection body, and its flag, the national registration a ship needs, and with them any right to run businesses on board. He wrote that assuming a stationary residential ship would be easy to insure had been incorrect. The ship was sold for scrap on 18 December 2020 and was to go on to India. Trade press later reported that it was arrested in Panama, meaning held by court order, then released and sold to a new cruise startup in 2021.
ms-satoshi.mechanism: A ship's legal status at sea depends in practice on private insurers. Without liability insurance a ship cannot keep a crew, a class rating or a flag, and so has no lawful standing.
ms-satoshi.stopped_by: Marine insurers; no protection and indemnity (liability) cover was available
ms-satoshi.challenge: It failed before any state acted

ms-the-world.story: MS The World is a private ship run like a block of flats, with 165 apartments and studios owned by the people who live on it. It was the idea of Knut Kloster, from a family long in the shipping business, and it was first announced as The World of ResidenSea, ordered in 2000 and completed on 20 February 2002. Its port of registry is Nassau in the Bahamas, which means the ship flies the Bahamian flag and Bahamian law applies on board at sea. ROW Management runs it from Fort Lauderdale, Florida. Residents come from many countries, and some live on board full-time while others visit from time to time. They elect a board that advises the management company on the route and finances. On average it carries 150 to 200 residents and guests, with a crew of about 280. It emptied in March 2020 because of COVID-19 and returned to service in July 2021. It makes no claim to statehood, and it keeps sailing as a working example of the ordinary legal route, a registered ship, a flag state and a private ownership agreement.
ms-the-world.mechanism: People can live permanently at sea with no claim to sovereignty by using an ordinary flag registration. The flag state, the country where the ship is registered, supplies the law on board.
ms-the-world.laws: Registered in the Bahamas, with Nassau as its port of registry
ms-the-world.challenge: Never tested, because it operates as an ordinary registered ship

pangeos-terayacht.story: Pangeos is a design by the design studio Lazzarini for what it calls a terayacht, a floating city shaped like a giant turtle. It would measure 550 metres long and 610 metres wide, which would make it the largest floating structure ever built, at a stated cost of $8 billion. It would hold hotels, shopping malls, apartments, parks and ports for smaller ships and aircraft, and it would float on 30,000 cells, sit 30 metres deep in the water and carry solar panels on its roof. Its cruising speed would be five knots, or about 9 kilometres an hour. No shipyard can build it now, so around one square kilometre of sea would need to be dredged and a circular dam built. The designers have named King Abdullah Port in Saudi Arabia as the site and hoped to start in 2033 with a build of eight years. A crowdfunding scheme sells virtual tickets and apartments, from $16 to $169, as NFTs, a kind of digital ownership record. A vessel of this kind would still need a flag, and CNN's report does not name one. Nothing has been built so far.
pangeos-terayacht.mechanism: However large, a vessel at sea is governed by the law of the country whose flag it flies. Pangeos would therefore be a very big ship under one state's law, and it would create no new territory.

set.anchor: King Abdullah Port, Saudi Arabia, where the designers propose to build it

radio-caroline.story: Radio Caroline was a pirate radio station that broadcast to Britain from ships anchored off the coast, outside British waters. In 1964 the BBC held a monopoly on radio in Britain. Ronan O'Rahilly, an Irish businessman who managed musicians, had failed to get his singer Georgie Fame played on the BBC or Radio Luxembourg, so he fitted out a ship, MV Caroline, as a radio station and anchored it off Felixstowe, Suffolk. Its first programme went out on 28 March 1964. That July it merged with Allan Crawford's rival Radio Atlanta, whose ship, MV Mi Amigo, became Radio Caroline South off Frinton-on-Sea. Because a ship in international waters lies outside a coastal state's territorial sea, the station needed no British licence. Governments answered with a treaty, the European Agreement for the Prevention of Broadcasts Transmitted from Stations outside National Territories. Britain applied it through the Marine, &c., Broadcasting (Offences) Act 1967, in force from 15 August 1967. The Act did not reach the ship itself. It made it illegal for British subjects to supply, advertise on or otherwise work with such a station. Caroline carried on from international waters using several ships in turn. Dutch authorities raided its last ship, the Ross Revenge, in August 1989, and broadcasts at sea stopped on 5 November 1990 for lack of fuel and supplies. It later broadcast by satellite and internet. In May 2017 Ofcom, the UK broadcasting regulator, awarded it a medium-wave community licence for Suffolk and north Essex, and it began full-time broadcasts on 648 kHz that December.
radio-caroline.mechanism: Britain could not reach a ship broadcasting from international waters, so it made rules for its own subjects. Banning them from supplying or advertising on the station avoided any decision about who governed the vessel.
radio-caroline.stopped_by: Britain's 1967 Marine Broadcasting Offences Act cut off British support; broadcasts at sea ended in 1990 for lack of fuel and supplies
radio-caroline.challenge: It kept broadcasting from international waters after 1967, but British subjects could no longer work with it
radio-caroline.why: Replaced 'five ships in turn', not found in the source, with 'several ships'. Added the 1989 raid and the 1990 cause of the end at sea.

radio-mercur.story: Radio Mercur was a pop music station that broadcast to Denmark from a ship anchored in international waters between 1958 and 1962, and it was probably the first commercial offshore radio station in the world. In summer 1958 Peer Jansen, a 27-year-old office trainee, and his cousin Børge Agerskov, a law student, had grown tired of the conservative music on Denmark's state radio. Agerskov noticed that radio in international waters was regulated only by international agreements, and those had not imagined a ship broadcasting regularly from anchor. The silver trader Ib Fogh supplied money. Regular broadcasts began on 2 August 1958 from the ship Cheeta Mercur in the Øresund, the strait between Denmark and Sweden, carrying pop music and advertising, with programmes taped in Copenhagen and carried out by boat. A larger ship, Cheeta II, later lay in the Great Belt. The station inspired Radio Veronica, Radio Nord and others, and Danish newspapers called it a pirate. In June 1962 the Danish parliament banned all participation in supporting such broadcasts from 1 August, and other Nordic countries passed similar laws. The station closed officially on 31 July 1962, with a last burst of broadcasts in mid-August.
radio-mercur.mechanism: Denmark had no power over a ship in international waters, so it made the work on land illegal. Recording programmes or supplying the ship from Danish soil became an offence, which ended the station.
radio-mercur.stopped_by: A Danish law passed in June 1962, in force from 1 August 1962

radio-nord.story: Radio Nord was a station that played American-style Top 40 pop in Swedish from a ship anchored in international waters of the Baltic Sea, with offices in central Stockholm. The Texan broadcaster Gordon McLendon and the investor Clint Murchison Jr. were among its backers. It began on 8 March 1961, six days after the Swedish Parliament passed laws letting officials seize the broadcasting equipment if the ship came back to a Swedish port. The ship, first called Olga, then Bon Jour and then Magda Maria, flew the flag of Nicaragua, meaning it was registered there. After Sweden pressed Nicaragua, the owners moved the registration to Panama. Sweden next banned selling advertising on the station, the part of the business that had to touch land. Radio Nord closed on 30 June 1962, a month before that law took effect. The ship sailed to Spain and was renamed Mi Amigo, and in 1964 it reappeared off Essex, England, as Radio Atlanta and then Radio Caroline South.
radio-nord.mechanism: A state cannot board a foreign-registered ship in open water, but it can act on what touches its own territory. Sweden used a power of seizure at port, pressure on the flag country and a ban on selling the station's advertising.
radio-nord.stopped_by: A Swedish ban on selling advertising for such stations, passed in 1962

radio-veronica.story: Radio Veronica was a Dutch pop radio station that broadcast from a ship off the coast of the Netherlands from 1960 to 1974. Dutch retailers of radios and appliances set it up to sell more receivers, by offering an alternative to the state-licensed stations in Hilversum. Regular broadcasts began on 6 May 1960 from a former lightship, Borkum Riff, anchored off the coast, with programmes recorded in Hilversum and taken out to it. It became the most popular station in the Netherlands. In 1964 the Dutch government passed a law against broadcasting from REM Island, an artificial structure at sea, and raided that island, but it left Veronica alone because of the station's popularity. A new ship, the trawler MV Norderney, took over that year. In May 1971 three men firebombed the rival ship Mebo II, and Veronica's directors were arrested. Parliament then drew up a ban. On 2 April 1973 Norderney lost its anchor in a storm and ran aground at Scheveningen, two weeks before a planned rally, and a rival ship carried its programmes. The law passed anyway, and Veronica shut at 6 pm on 31 August 1974, hours before it took effect.
radio-veronica.mechanism: A government can tolerate a station at sea for years and then close it by law on land. The Dutch ended Veronica after 14 years by banning anyone from supplying offshore stations from shore.
radio-veronica.stopped_by: A Dutch law in force from 1 September 1974

rni-mebo-ii.story: Radio North Sea International (RNI) was an offshore pop station run from the ship Mebo II, off the coasts of the Netherlands and Britain, by two Swiss engineers, Edwin Bollier and Erwin Meister. They bought the 630-tonne ship Silvretta in 1969 and renamed it. It carried a 105-kilowatt medium-wave transmitter, the strongest on any pirate ship. Regular broadcasts began on 11 February 1970. In March the ship moved to 5 miles off Clacton, in international waters. From 15 April the British government jammed its signal, and RNI campaigned against the Labour government in that June's election. It went back to the Dutch coast in July. On 29 August a tug tried to take over the ship, and the crew armed themselves with knives and petrol bombs while appealing for help on air. RNI closed on 24 September in return for 1 million guilders from its rival Radio Veronica, then returned in January 1971. On 15 May 1971 a bomb set the ship on fire, and all five people convicted received a year in prison. That attack convinced the Dutch to ban supplying such stations from land, in force from 1 September 1974, and the station closed. Libya bought the ships in 1977.
rni-mebo-ii.mechanism: States could not board a foreign-owned ship in open water, so they acted from outside it. Britain jammed its signal, and the Netherlands later cut off its supplies from shore.
rni-mebo-ii.stopped_by: The Dutch Marine Offences Act, from 1 September 1974

sea-shepherd-piracy.story: Sea Shepherd Conservation Society is an environmental group founded by Paul Watson in 1977 that uses ships to confront whalers. In the Southern Ocean it clashed with Japanese researchers who hunted whales under a research permit issued by Japan. The researchers sued it in the United States under the Alien Tort Statute, a law that lets foreigners bring certain claims in US courts, and argued that it was committing piracy. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea defines piracy as illegal violence on the high seas committed for private ends by the crew of a private ship against another ship. The trial court refused to order Sea Shepherd to stop and dismissed the piracy claim, limiting 'private ends' to financial gain. On 25 February 2013 the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed that decision. Chief Judge Kozinski wrote, 'You don't need a peg leg or an eye patch.' He listed ramming ships, throwing glass containers of acid, dragging ropes to damage propellers and pointing high-powered lasers at other ships. The court said 'private' is normally the opposite of 'public' and is far broader than money. It later held Sea Shepherd in contempt over attacks by foreign affiliates, and in 2015 the group agreed to pay $2.55 million. A settlement announced on 23 August 2016 permanently barred it and Watson from attacking the whalers or coming within 500 yards of their ships on the open sea. Watson, who had left Sea Shepherd, was arrested in Greenland in July 2024 on a Japanese warrant and freed on 17 December 2024 after Denmark rejected extradition.
sea-shepherd-piracy.mechanism: In 2013 a US appeal court read 'private ends' in the international definition of piracy to include goals beyond money. Under that ruling, attacks by private ships on the high seas can count as piracy even when activists carry them out for a cause.
sea-shepherd-piracy.stopped_by: The US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled for the whalers
sea-shepherd-piracy.challenge: It lost in the US appeal court, which called its acts piracy
